title: Overview of Cloud Computing
overview: Learn what cloud computing is, why organisations adopt it, and how service models divide operational responsibility. Compare deployment models and the cloud-hosted, optimised and native approaches. Use these distinctions to justify a workload-specific strategy rather than assuming cloud always saves money.
big_ideas: Cloud provides on-demand network access to pooled, configurable resources that can be rapidly provisioned and metered.
Five NIST essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.
Economies of scale can lower provider unit costs; customer savings still depend on workload and design.
IaaS = you manage OS and up; PaaS = you manage app and data; SaaS = you manage only settings and your data.
Deployment models: public, private, hybrid, multi-cloud, VPC, proprietary; hybrid mixes cloud types, multi-cloud mixes providers.
Cloud-hosted minimises initial change; cloud-native exploits elasticity and automation, with portability depending on the services chosen.
Cloud is not automatically cheaper, more secure or less secure; virtualisation alone is not a private cloud.
A cloud strategy needs business involvement, an exit strategy and sensible first workloads, not just an executive mandate.

sections.title: Cloud characteristics and economies of scale
sections.summary: The technologies and philosophy behind cloud, the NIST definition with its five essential characteristics, and the economics that make providers efficient.

notes.h: Cloud is a service model for resources
items: **On-demand access** to a **shared pool** of resources
**Rapidly provisioned and released**
**Private clouds** can be operated by the organisation itself
**On-demand self-service**
**Broad network access**
**Resource pooling**
**Rapid elasticity**
**Measured service**: usage is monitored and reported → **pay-per-use** is a common pricing model
notes.foot: **Virtualisation alone** does not establish all five characteristics.

notes.h: Economies of scale lower unit cost
items: **Standardised workloads**
**Repeatable infrastructure**
**Bulk hardware**
**Streamlined software**
notes.foot: Lower provider costs do **not guarantee a lower customer bill**.

terms.def: Service-Oriented Architecture: systems built from network-callable services; one cloud pillar.
Resources scale out or in quickly to match demand.
Provider resources shared across many tenants, with location hidden from the customer.
Resource usage is monitored, controlled and reported, supporting transparency and usage-based charging.
Unit cost falls as the provider runs a huge, standardised infrastructure.

check.q: A virtualised server farm is provisioned by ticket and billed annually. What can you conclude about its NIST characteristics?

items: **Rapid elasticity**: check whether resources scale rapidly
**Measured service**: check whether usage is metered
**Annual billing alone** does not prove that elasticity or measured service is absent

check.q: A CFO argues: 'Providers have economies of scale, so moving our steady 24/7 batch servers to the cloud must cut our bill.' Do you agree?

items: **Economies of scale** (standardised workloads, bulk hardware, stripped-down software) lower the **provider's** unit cost
**Steady 24/7 load** → gains little from **elasticity** or paying only when needed
**Compare total cost** and operational needs for this workload
a.foot: The case is stronger if load is **spiky** or the team wants to **stop running hardware**.

check.q: An internal platform lets departments create VMs from a portal in minutes and sends each department a monthly usage report, but it can only be reached from managed office desktops. Which NIST characteristic is in doubt, and which ones can't you judge yet?

items: **Look satisfied**: **self-service** and **measured service**
**In doubt: broad network access** → it expects access over the network through **standard mechanisms** from **varied clients**
**Internal-only is not the problem** → **private clouds** are valid
**Still unknown: resource pooling and rapid elasticity** → until you know whether capacity is shared and can grow and shrink quickly

sections.title: Definitions of cloud computing
sections.summary: Definitions emphasise on-demand, scalable services delivered over a network. NIST provides a common test that also applies to private clouds.

items: **On-demand** resources
**Networked** resources
**Shared** resources
**Scalable** resources
Definitions **differ in emphasis**
**External providers** and **pay-per-use pricing** are common arrangements, **not requirements** of every private cloud
**IBM** → elastic, metered, self-service
**Gartner** → massive scalability for multiple external customers (**multi-tenancy**)
**IEEE** → data living on servers and **cached on many client devices**
**NIST** → the most-cited, **precise** definition
**Anchor on NIST**

terms.def: US standards body whose definition and five characteristics are the reference for cloud.
Capability consumed on demand from a provider instead of owned.

check.q: A hosting firm rents fixed physical servers on 12-month contracts, reachable over the internet, and markets them as 'cloud'. Using the common thread of the cloud definitions, is the label justified?

items: **Internet access** gives only **network access**
**Common thread** of the definitions: **on-demand** provisioning from a **shared pool**, **rapidly provisioned and released** with **minimal provider interaction**
**Fixed servers on long contracts** → neither **elastic** nor **on demand**
a.foot: The label would hold if customers could **self-provision and release** capacity in minutes and **pay for what they use**.

check.q: A teammate says an internal private cloud is 'not real cloud' because one industry definition describes cloud as a service delivered to many external customers. How do you respond?

items: **Gartner**'s wording emphasises **multi-tenant** delivery to **external customers**
**NIST**, the anchor definition, is about **characteristics**, not who operates it

items.t: **A private cloud for one organisation is cloud** if it offers:

sections.title: Why adopt cloud: benefits, barriers, trend
sections.summary: The business and technical reasons for adopting cloud, the obstacles enterprises face, and how cloud became mainstream.

items: **Faster provisioning** and **experimentation**
**Lower upfront investment**
**Elasticity** instead of owning **peak capacity**
**Automation and managed services** can improve **efficiency and resilience** when configured well
notes.foot: Compare **total cost and operational needs** rather than assuming every workload saves money.

notes.h: Why it is harder for enterprises
items: **Startups** → **cloud-first** with a clean slate; focus on **products**
**Enterprises** → cloud as a **strategic enabler**; focus on **migration, integration and co-existence**
**Most digital disruption** uses cloud in some form
**Large enterprises** such as **DBS Bank** are moving rapidly
notes.foot: The question has shifted from **whether to how**.

terms.def: Up-front capital spending on assets such as servers.
Ongoing operating expense, such as pay-per-use cloud bills.
Buying capacity for the highest expected load, which sits idle otherwise; cloud avoids it.
Running legacy on-premises systems alongside cloud ones during and after migration.

check.q: A startup expects anywhere between 1,000 and 200,000 users in its first year. Why does pay-as-you-go matter more to it than to a firm with flat, predictable load?

items: **Uncertain demand** → buying for peak means either a **large upfront investment** or **running out of capacity**
**Elasticity and usage-based spend** → cost follows actual users and makes **experiments cheap**
**Flat load** → the firm can size owned capacity accurately, so its gain from converting **CapEx to OpEx** is smaller
That gain has to be shown with a **total-cost comparison**

check.q: A bank and a fintech startup both want to launch a new payments feature on the cloud. Why will the bank's first-year plan look different?

sub: carries **regulatory, governance, security and privacy** obligations
**legacy systems** must be **migrated, integrated and co-exist** with the new feature

items: **Startup**: starts **cloud-first** on a **clean slate** → spends its effort on the product
**Bank's advantage**: existing **customers and data** → why integration is worth the cost

sections.title: Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
sections.summary: What a cloud service is, the three service models, and how responsibility shifts from customer to provider.

notes.h: Service models: who manages which layer
items: **IaaS = host**
**PaaS = build**
**SaaS = consume**
Each step up hands **more of the stack to the provider** → customer gets **less control** and **less operational work**
**IaaS** rents **compute, storage and network** (usually **virtual machines**); you control the **OS, middleware and apps**
**PaaS** gives a ready **solution stack** for building and deploying in the cloud; you control **only your deployed app**
**PaaS constraint**: the provider's **supported languages and tools** apply
**Choose IaaS** → need **OS-level control**
**Choose PaaS** → want to **ship code without running servers**
**PaaS** → you **write and own the application**
**SaaS** → you **rent a finished application** through a **browser**; change **only predefined settings**
**SaaS evolved from** **COTS** packages (like **SAP**) plus the **ASP** hosting model

notes.lead: Nine layers: data, applications, runtime, middleware, OS, virtualisation, servers, storage, networking.
items: **On-premises** → customer manages **all nine**
**IaaS** → provider takes **virtualisation downwards**
**PaaS** → provider adds **runtime, middleware and OS**
**SaaS** → provider covers **nearly everything**; the provider **operates the data service**
**Remain customer duties**: **data classification**, **access decisions**, **accountability**

terms.def: Rented compute, storage, network; you manage OS and above (e.g. AWS EC2).
Provider runs infrastructure and OS/runtime; you deploy code (e.g. Google App Engine).
Complete application used via browser (e.g. Office 365).
Commercial Off-The-Shelf packaged software.
Application Service Provider: earlier hosted-software model, ancestor of SaaS.
Split of management duties between customer and provider, shifting toward the provider from IaaS to SaaS.

check.q: A team must apply a specific OS kernel patch and install custom middleware. Which service model fits, and what extra work comes with it?

a.lead: **IaaS**: the only model where the customer controls the **OS and middleware**.
items: **Extra work**: the team now **patches the OS**, **runs the middleware** and **configures scaling** itself
**If the kernel requirement went away** → **PaaS** would remove that work
a.foot: In return for PaaS you accept the provider's **supported languages and runtimes**.

check.q: An HR department needs leave management. A standard product covers 90% of its workflow, but there is one unusual approval rule. SaaS or an app built on PaaS?

a.lead: **SaaS** if the rule can be expressed through the product's **predefined settings**.
items: **SaaS** → gives the **least operational work**
**Build on PaaS** only if the rule is **essential** and **cannot be configured** → you write and **own the application** but avoid running servers
a.foot: Deciding factor: whether the **customisation is worth owning code for**.

check.q: Customer data leaks from a SaaS CRM because an employee shared a report with a public link. The team blames the provider. Who is accountable?

items: Even in **SaaS**, where the provider operates nearly every layer, **data classification**, **access decisions** and **accountability** stay with the customer
a.foot: Would differ if the leak came from a **breach of the provider's own infrastructure or application**, which are its layers.

visuals.title: Who manages what (ISO 27018): customer vs public cloud provider
visuals.caption: Simplified operational split. Providers still have data-protection duties; customers retain classification and access responsibilities.

sections.title: Deployment models
sections.summary: Who owns and operates the cloud and who shares it: public, private, hybrid, multi-cloud, VPC and proprietary.

notes.h: Deployment models: who owns, operates, shares
items: **Public** → **provider-owned**, open to anyone, **multi-tenant** with **logical data separation**
**Private** → operated **solely for one organisation**; **on-premises or off**; run by it or a **third party**
**Hybrid** → **interconnects two or more cloud types** (e.g. private plus public) that **stay distinct**
**Multi-cloud** → **multiple providers**, usually several **public** clouds
**VPC** → **carved out of a provider's infrastructure**; keeps **public-cloud scalability and pricing**, adds **isolation and controlled access**
**Proprietary cloud** → a **packaged hardware plus software stack**, **provider-owned** or **sold for on-premises** use
**Public** → **shared managed capacity**
**Private** → **organisation-exclusive** infrastructure
**Hybrid** → systems must **span private and public** environments
**VPC** → **logical network isolation** within a public cloud
notes.foot: A VPC does **not** make the infrastructure **on-premises** or **automatically compliant**.

terms.def: Many customers share the same infrastructure with logical data separation.
Virtual Private Cloud: isolated, access-controlled section of a provider's cloud.
Interconnected mix of cloud types, e.g. private plus public.
Use of several cloud providers.

check.q: A company runs its core system in its own data centre and its analytics on two public providers. A teammate calls this 'multi-cloud'. Is that the full description?

items: **Multi-cloud**: two public providers (mixing **vendors**)
**Hybrid**: connecting them to the **on-premises private** environment (mixing **cloud types**)

sub: hybrid → **integration and co-existence** concerns between environments

check.q: A team proposes a VPC to meet the rule 'customer data must not leave our premises'. Does it?

items: **VPC** = **logical network isolation** and **controlled access** inside the **provider's infrastructure** → data still sits on the **provider's premises**
**The rule calls for** a **private cloud**, or a **hybrid** design that keeps that data on premises
a.foot: A VPC fits when the requirement is **isolation with public-cloud scalability and pricing**, not **data location**.

check.q: A vendor offers a pre-integrated rack of hardware and cloud software to install in your data centre. Which deployment model is this, and how does it compare with building your own private cloud?

items: **What it is**: a complete **hardware plus software stack**, owned by the provider or sold for **on-premises** use
**vs your own private cloud**: **faster to stand up** than assembling one from parts
**But** you depend on that **vendor's stack** for upgrades and features

sections.title: Major providers
sections.summary: The leading providers all offer a broad catalogue spanning the same categories.

notes.lead: AWS, Azure and GCP all cover:
items: **Compute**
**Networking**
**Storage and databases**
**Big data**
**Identity and security**
**Machine learning**
**Management and developer tooling**

notes.h: Think in categories, not product names

items.t: **Map each need** to the relevant provider service:

items: **Justify the choice** in an architecture answer
**IaaS** → **control**
**PaaS** → **productivity**
**FaaS/serverless** → **event-driven** code
notes.foot: Later topics (**reference architectures**, **serverless**) build on choosing among them.

terms.def: Amazon Web Services, a cloud provider offering infrastructure and managed application services.
Microsoft's cloud platform.
Google Cloud Platform.

check.q: An exam answer for a web app's architecture says only 'use EC2, S3, RDS and CloudFront'. Why would it lose marks, and how should it be rewritten?

a.lead: It lists **product names** without the **need** each one meets or **why** it was chosen.
items: **Justify each choice** from the requirements
Major providers have **overlapping categories** → the **reasoning** carries the marks, not the product name

check.q: Two providers both cover compute, storage, databases, identity, ML and management tooling. Your client wants to pick one by comparing catalogue size. What should decide it instead?

items: **Decide from** the workload's **requirements** and the **cloud strategy**
**Finish the strategy before signing vendor contracts** (**Gartner** lists this as a common mistake)
**Keep an exit strategy**
**Favour containers and open standards** where **switching cost** matters

sections.title: Development options, myths and strategy mistakes
sections.summary: How applications can be placed on the cloud, plus Gartner's myths and strategy mistakes that warn against naive adoption.

items: **Cloud-hosted** → moves an existing app with **little change**
**Cloud-optimised** → **adapts selected components**
**Cloud-native** → designs for **elasticity, resilience and automation**; often needs **more redesign and skills**
notes.foot: Lecture comparison: deeper use of **proprietary services** → **reduced backward portability**.

notes.h: Benefits and lock-in depend on choices
items: **Managed proprietary APIs** → may increase **switching cost**
**Containers and open standards** → can **preserve portability**
**Cloud-native designs** can also run in **private and hybrid** clouds
Cloud **always saves money**
You **must be on cloud to be good**
Use it **for everything**
**'The CEO said so'** is a strategy
You need **one provider**
It is **less secure**
It is **not for mission-critical**
**Cloud = data centre**
**Migration automatically yields all benefits**
**Virtualisation = private cloud**
**Confusing strategy with an implementation plan**, or **excluding business**
**No exit strategy**
**Assuming all benefits** without prioritising
Expecting **multicloud** to **save money or improve DR**
**Cloud-first read as cloud-only**
**Starting with critical complex workloads** like **ERP**
Treating an **executive mandate** as strategy
**Too broad a scope**
**Signing vendor contracts** before the strategy is done
**Outsourcing the strategy**

terms.def: Lift and shift: existing app runs on cloud infrastructure with minimal change.
Existing app modified to use some cloud services directly.
Application designed for cloud properties such as elasticity, resilience and automation; portability depends on its dependencies.
Plan for leaving or switching provider.
New system built from scratch with no legacy constraints.

check.q: A team has 3 months to leave a data centre whose lease is ending. The application has stable load and no planned changes. Cloud-hosted or cloud-native?

items: **Minimal change** → the only way to meet the deadline
**Stable load** → gains little from **elasticity**
a.foot: Gives up the **resilience, autoscaling and automation** gains of a redesign, but selected components can be made **cloud-optimised** later, once the deadline is met.

check.q: The CEO announces: 'We are cloud-first. Every system moves next year, starting with our ERP.' Critique this as a strategy.

a.lead: It makes several of **Gartner's mistakes** at once:
items: **Executive mandate** treated as a strategy
**Cloud-first** read as **cloud-only**
**Starting with a critical, complex workload** like ERP

check.q: A security officer says: 'Cloud is less secure, so mission-critical systems must stay on premises.' Do you agree?

items: **'Less secure'** and **'not for mission-critical'** are both listed **cloud myths**
**Security depends on design** and on the **responsibility split**
**Provider** secures its layers; the **customer** must still secure its own **configuration, identities and data**
a.foot: A specific **regulatory or data-location constraint**, not the myth, is the valid reason to keep a system on premises.

check.q: A team builds heavily on one provider's proprietary queue and database APIs to go cloud-native quickly. What risk are they taking, and how could they limit it?

a.lead: **Risk**: deep use of proprietary services raises **switching cost** and reduces **portability**.
items: **Limit it**: **containers and open standards** where they matter
**Isolate provider-specific calls** behind their own interfaces
**Keep an exit strategy**
a.foot: Trade-off: avoiding **managed proprietary services** gives up some of the **speed** that made cloud-native attractive.

visuals.title: Levels of cloud adaptation

steps.label: Cloud-hosted
steps.detail: Run in the cloud; low effort; infrastructure modernization. Leverages cloud attributes only indirectly, limited additional benefits; nearly complete backward portability.

steps.label: Cloud-optimised
steps.detail: Grow in the cloud; moderate extension effort; application modernization. Leverages cloud attributes directly, moderate benefits; reduced backward portability.

steps.label: Cloud-native
steps.detail: Design for elasticity, resilience and automation. Greater redesign and new skills may be needed; proprietary dependencies reduce portability, while open standards can help preserve it.

visuals.caption: Alternative levels of change, not mandatory migration stages.

exam_angles.q: A retailer runs a 6-week seasonal web shop. Evening traffic is 20 times the daytime level, the team is two developers, and there is no ops staff. Recommend a service model and a deployment model, and say what would make you choose IaaS instead.

a.lead: **PaaS on a public cloud**, with **SaaS** for commodity parts such as **payments or email**.
items: **PaaS** → the provider runs the **OS and runtime**
**Elasticity** → absorbs the **evening peaks** without the retailer owning peak capacity
**Spend follows the 6-week season** instead of a **year-round investment**
a.foot: **Choose IaaS** only if the shop needs **OS-level control** or **middleware** the platform doesn't support, and accept that the **two developers** would then **patch and scale servers** themselves.

exam_angles.q: A regulated bank must keep customer records in its own data centre but wants elastic capacity for a new customer-facing app. Recommend a deployment model, and explain why a VPC alone is not enough.

items: **Customer records** stay in the **on-premises private environment**
**Elastic front end** runs on **public cloud**
Connected through **controlled integration**
**VPC alone is not enough** → **logical isolation** inside the **provider's infrastructure**, but does not keep data on the **bank's premises**
a.foot: Costs: **governance, integration and co-existence** work across two environments, plus the **latency** of calls back to on-premises data.

exam_angles.q: An enterprise wants its first cloud project to be moving its 15-year-old, heavily customised ERP. Advise on whether it should go first, and compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS for it when it does move.

sub: **Gartner** warns against starting with **critical, complex, large** workloads like ERP
**IaaS** (**cloud-hosted lift and shift**): keeps the **customisation**, needs the **least change**, but keeps all the **OS and middleware** work
**SaaS**: removes most of the **operations** but forces the business onto **predefined settings** → may mean dropping **years of customisation**

exam_angles.q: A proposal says: 'Move to the cloud to save money, and use two providers so disaster recovery is automatic.' Evaluate both claims and say what evidence you would want.

items: **Cloud is not always cheaper**
**Multi-cloud** does not by itself **save money** or **improve DR** → it adds **cross-provider skills and operations**
a.foot: Multi-cloud may still be justified for **specific reasons**, but it should come with an **exit strategy** rather than an assumed benefit.

exam_angles.q: An IT department rebrands its virtualisation cluster as 'our private cloud'. Developers can create VMs from a portal in minutes, but capacity is fixed at 200 VMs, adding hosts takes a 6-week purchase, and there is no usage reporting. Assess the claim against NIST and recommend what would close the gaps.

items: **On-demand self-service**: met by the **portal**
**Resource pooling**: a **shared cluster** suggests it
**Rapid elasticity**: fails → the **200-VM cap** and **6-week purchase** stop capacity from growing quickly
**Measured service**: fails → nothing is **metered**
**Virtualisation alone is not a private cloud**

sub: either keep **spare capacity** or **burst to public cloud** (a **hybrid** model) so capacity can grow on demand
